result: The study measured environmental conditions experienced by wandering albatrosses during take-off using animal-borne sensors, finding wind speeds ranged from 0.7 to 15.4 m/s (mean 6.5 ± 2.7 m/s) and wave heights from 1.6 to 6.4 m (mean 3.0 ± 0.8 m). Westerly winds were frequently observed, consistent with previous observations around the breeding colony.
evaluation: All reviewers praised the use of animal-borne data-loggers to generate 'a compelling high quality dataset on animal movement and environmental conditions.' Reviewers explicitly stated the methods provide 'new insight' and that the authors 'achieved their aims' with results that 'support their conclusions.' No concerns were raised about the environmental measurements.

result: The study characterized take-off behavior parameters including running duration (mean 5.1 ± 1.5 s, range 1.1-11.7 s), running speed (mean 6.5 ± 1.6 m/s), flapping number (mean 4.3, range 0 to >20), and flapping frequency (mean 2.55 ± 0.29 Hz). Males had slightly higher running speeds than females (p < 0.01), but no significant sex differences were found for other parameters.
evaluation: Reviewers stated the authors 'provide novel quantitative data on this behavior' and that 'results were impressive, presented well.' One reviewer noted a weakness that 'interpretation of accelerometry data was not validated using a subset of the sample synchronized with video,' but this did not prevent acceptance of the findings, as reviewers concluded the authors 'achieved their aims' and results 'support their conclusions.'

result: Wandering albatrosses tended to take-off with headwinds (p < 0.01), but cruising direction did not correlate with headwind direction, indicating birds face the wind on take-off regardless of destination. The mean air speed at the end of the running phase was 12.2 ± 3.1 m/s, close to average flight speed and predicted best glide speeds, indicating efficient wind utilization.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged that 'it is generally understood that albatross and many other birds choose to takeoff into the wind,' but praised the authors for providing 'novel quantitative data on this behavior.' One reviewer noted the 'interpretation of wind direction relative to flight path is based on the behavior of the bird without concurrent measures of local wind velocity,' but this methodological limitation did not prevent acceptance of the conclusions.

result: Running duration, running speed, and flapping number all significantly decreased as wind speed and wave height increased. Albatrosses tended to flap fewer times under stronger wind conditions, and take-offs in wave heights below 2 m always required flapping. The trend of flapping frequency with wave height remained unclear.
evaluation: Reviewers stated the results on 'the effects of wave height and the interactions between wave height and wind provide novel insight' and that the authors 'revealed that each of these factors contributes to take-off in a unique way with interesting interactions.' The acknowledgment of uncertainty about flapping frequency trends was not criticized, and reviewers concluded results 'support their conclusions.'

result: Take-off was easier under higher wave conditions than under lower wave conditions at constant wind speed, and take-off effort increased only when both wind and waves were gentle. Statistical modeling showed wind speed, wave height, and their interaction best explained take-off parameters. Under weak wind (2 m/s), running duration decreased from 8 to 4 s as wave height increased, while under strong wind (8 m/s), low running duration was maintained regardless of wave height.
evaluation: This represents the core novel finding of the paper. Reviewers emphasized that 'the new insight into the effects of wave height should revise understanding among ornithologists, ocean ecologists and those who study the mechanics of animal locomotion.' All reviewers stated the authors 'achieved their objectives' and 'results support their conclusions.' The statistical approach and interaction effects were not questioned.

result: The study concludes that both ocean waves and winds play important roles for albatross take-off, advancing understanding of albatross flight mechanisms. Environmental variables estimated using animal-borne recorders provide valuable insight when mathematical weather models are too coarse. The findings demonstrate that wind speed is not the only parameter influencing flight decisions, and wave height should be included in future studies.
evaluation: Reviewers unanimously praised these conclusions. One stated this work 'will set new standards in integrating information about bird movement and environmental conditions' and provides 'heuristic insights for many additional systems.' Another noted the research 'provides worthwhile new insight into how wind and wave action affect takeoff' with implications for understanding climate change effects. All reviewers confirmed the authors 'achieved their aims' and conclusions are supported.

result: The study infers that running behavior entails large energetic costs because albatrosses must reach fast initial speeds by rapidly moving hindlimbs for up to ~10 s in unfavorable conditions. Wandering albatrosses likely undertake high-frequency flapping only during the running phase as they lift off, then continue with moderate flapping frequency until reaching flight stability.
evaluation: These interpretations about energetic costs and flapping patterns were not challenged by reviewers. Reviewers stated the authors 'provide convincing set of results that support the aims and conclusions' and that the paper was 'generally written in an accessible way.' The inferences about energetic implications align with the reviewers' emphasis on the study's contributions to understanding 'bio-energetics.'

result: The reduced running behavior and flapping under strong wind conditions are explained by the lift force mechanism, where lift is proportional to the square of air speed. Previous studies on European shag and wandering albatrosses found take-off direction biased toward headwinds, though prior work acknowledged limitations in mathematical weather models and GPS resolution.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these mechanistic explanations without criticism. One reviewer explicitly noted 'it is generally understood that albatross and many other birds choose to takeoff into the wind to reduce energetic costs,' indicating acceptance of the lift force mechanism. The acknowledgment of prior study limitations was not contested.

result: The study discusses potential mechanisms by which waves aid take-off, including wave-slope soaring (updrafts from wave topography) and the possibility that rough ocean surface provides favorable bumps for launching. However, the authors acknowledge the mechanism is not entirely clear and other unresolved mechanisms may exist.
evaluation: Reviewers did not explicitly evaluate these speculative mechanistic explanations. While reviewers praised the demonstration that 'ocean waves aid the most energy-consuming behavior, take-off,' they did not comment on the proposed mechanisms. The authors' own acknowledgment of uncertainty ('mechanism...is not entirely clear') suggests appropriate caution, but reviewers neither affirmed nor challenged these speculations.

result: The introduction establishes that the relationship between environment and marine animal small-scale behavior is not fully understood due to difficulty obtaining high spatiotemporal precision environmental data. Previous seabird research relied on ocean climatic models rather than in situ observations, and seabird take-off has never been effectively investigated despite being potentially affected by environmental conditions.
evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accepted this framing of the research gap. One reviewer stated the study addresses 'the complex and challenging environment in which albatross live' and another noted the approach provides insights 'where organisms are influenced by, and respond to small-scale environmental conditions.' The motivation for using animal-borne sensors to overcome limitations of mathematical models was endorsed by all reviewers.

result: The study obtained 1477 hr of data from 44 wandering albatrosses in 2019 and 2020, identifying 703 take-offs. After filtering for flight duration and floating time, 185 take-offs had both wind and wave conditions estimated. Small recorders (28 g, 0.3-0.4% body mass) and large recorders (91 g, 0.8-1.3% body mass) were used, with previous studies showing no negative impacts on breeding or foraging at <3% body mass.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the dataset as 'compelling' and 'high quality.' One reviewer noted 'there is no better platform for this initial work because these birds are so large, the equipment they can carry without creating significant impact is tremendous.' The methodological details and sample sizes were not questioned, and reviewers stated the authors 'achieved their aims.'
